title: Standard form
task: Express 7200000 in standard form, then divide it by 0.0003. Explain how the powers of ten change.
solution: 7.2 × 10⁶; the quotient is 2.4 × 10¹⁰.

title: Arithmetic sequences and finite sums
task: For deposits 10, 15, 20, … write the tenth term and the sum of ten deposits using sigma notation.
solution: u₁₀=55; Σ from k=1 to 10 of [10+5(k−1)] = 325. A constant difference distinguishes this from geometric growth.

title: Geometric sequences and finite sums
task: Compare the first four terms and sums when u₁=8 and r=0.5 or r=−0.5.
solution: Positive ratio: 8, 4, 2, 1, sum 15. Negative ratio: 8, −4, 2, −1, sum 5. These are finite sums.

title: Compound growth, depreciation and inflation
task: Compare 1000 invested at 6% nominal annual interest compounded annually and monthly over one year. Then account for 3% inflation.
solution: Annual:1060; monthly:1000(1.005)¹²≈1061.68. Divide each by 1.03 to express purchasing power in starting-year money.

title: Integer powers and logarithms
task: Simplify (2³×2⁻¹)/2². Rewrite eˣ=7 using a logarithm and use technology to find x.
solution: The quotient is 2⁰=1. x=ln 7≈1.94591. Exponential and logarithmic forms express the same relationship.

title: Approximation, bounds and error
task: A rectangle has sides 8.4 and 3.2 cm, both rounded to 0.1 cm. Bound its area. If an estimate is 27cm² and the exact area is 26.88cm², calculate percentage error.
solution: 26.3025≤area<27.4625cm². Percentage error=100|27−26.88|/26.88≈0.446429%. State precision and check the order of magnitude before accepting a calculation.

title: Loans and annuities
task: For a 1000 loan at 1% per month, pay 100 at each month-end. Calculate the first two balances and explain how an annuity reverses the cash-flow direction.
solution: 910 then 819.10. Each month first multiply the balance by 1.01, then subtract 100. Savings with end-of-period deposits instead add 100; timing matters.

title: Systems and polynomial equations
task: Solve x+y=7 and 2x−y=2, then use the cubic explorer to find every solution of x³−3x=2. Verify by substitution.
solution: x=3, y=4. Cubic roots are−1 (repeated) and 2. A graph can touch an axis without crossing it; sign-change searches alone miss repeated roots.

title: Straight-line equations
task: Find the line through(1, 5) parallel to y=2x+1, then the perpendicular line through the same point. Express the first in general form.
solution: y=2x+3, or 2x−y+3=0. The perpendicular is y−5=−0.5(x−1). Horizontal and vertical lines need separate handling.

title: Functions, domains, ranges and inverses
task: Restrict f(x)=2x+3 to 0≤x≤4. State its range and inverse, including the inverse domain, and interpret f⁻¹(f(2)).
solution: Range[3, 11]; f⁻¹(x)=(x−3)/2 on[3, 11]. f⁻¹(f(2))=2: the inverse undoes the function.

title: Graphs and combinations
task: Sketch f=x²−4, g=2x+1, f+g and f−g. Label intercepts and vertices; compare your sketch with the explorer.
solution: f+g=x²+2x−3 has vertex(−1, −4), zeros−3, 1. f−g=x²−2x−5 has vertex(1, −6), zeros 1±√6.

title: Graph features and intersections
task: Find the vertex, symmetry axis, intercepts and intersections with y=1 of y=(x−2)²−3. Then inspect the asymptotes of y=2/x.
solution: Vertex(2, −3), axis x=2, y-intercept 1, zeros 2±√3; y=1 at x=0, 4. For 2/x the asymptotes arex=0, y=0.

title: Linear, quadratic, exponential, power, cubic and periodic models
task: Choose models for a two-rate taxi tariff, a cooling object, inverse sharing and seasonal temperature. For T=8 sin(30x)+12 in degrees, state amplitude, period and principal axis.
solution: Piecewise linear; exponential decay with offset; inverse proportion; sinusoidal. T has amplitude 8, period 12 and principal axis T=12. Explain the meaning and units of each parameter.

title: Building and evaluating models
task: Fit y=ax²+bx+c through(0, 1), (1, 4), (2, 9) using simultaneous equations. A new observation is(3, 15). Calculate its residual, then discuss a sensible domain and whether to revise the model.
solution: c=1, a+b=3, 4a+2b=8 gives a=1, b=2, c=1. Predicted 16; observed−predicted residual−1. Validation requires new observations and context, not just fitting the original points.

title: Three-dimensional measurement and solids
task: A cylinder of radius 2 and height 5 has a hemisphere of radius 2 attached on top. Find total volume and exposed area, including the bottom. Also find distance and midpoint from(0, 0, 0) to(2, 4, 5).
solution: Volume=20π+16π/3=76π/3. External area=20π+8π+4π=32π; omit the shared circular face. Distance√45; midpoint(1, 2, 2.5).

title: Right and non-right triangles
task: For sides 5 and 7 with included angle 60°, find the third side and area. Explain why some side-side-angle information gives two triangles.
solution: Third side√39; area 35sin60°/2≈15.1554. Since sinB=sin(180°−B), two positive remaining-angle solutions may be possible.

title: Bearings and angles of elevation or depression
task: A boat travels 10 km on bearing 030°. Find east and north displacement and its return bearing. Sketch a 20m tower viewed from 40m away on level ground; find the depression angle from its top.
solution: East 5 km, north 5√3 km, return 210°. Depression=arctan(20/40)≈26.5651°, equal to the elevation angle from the ground by parallel horizontals.

title: Arcs and sectors in degrees
task: For radius 6 and angle 120°, calculate arc length, sector area and sector perimeter.
solution: Arc 4π; area 12π; perimeter 12+4π. The angle is one third of a complete turn.

title: Perpendicular bisectors
task: Find the perpendicular bisector of A(2, 1), B(6, 5). Verify that(4, 3) and(3, 4) are equidistant from A and B.
solution: Midpoint(4, 3), segment slope 1; bisector y=−x+7. Squared distances are 8 at the midpoint and 10 at(3, 4).

title: Voronoi diagrams and nearest-site decisions
task: Add the third site in the region explorer. Identify cells, shared edges and the triple vertex. Explain where a new service station could reduce the greatest distance to an existing station.
solution: Each cell contains points nearest its site; shared edges are parts of perpendicular bisectors. A triple vertex is equidistant from three sites. For a bounded service area, compare Voronoi vertices, edge-boundary intersections and boundary corners; justify practical constraints.

title: Data quality and sampling
task: Design a stratified sample of 20 from 60 younger and 40 older people. Contrast it with convenience sampling and identify two possible sources of unreliable data.
solution: Randomly select 12 younger and 8 older people. Convenience selection may systematically exclude groups. Non-response, unclear questions, recording errors and outdated sources can undermine reliability; counts are discrete and measured times continuous.

title: Tables, histograms, cumulative frequency and box plots
task: For frequencies 4, 8, 8, 4 in intervals[0, 10), [10, 20), [20, 30), [30, 40), estimate the 75 th percentile from the cumulative graph. Compare box plots before and after increasing the extreme value.
solution: Cumulative counts 4, 12, 20, 24; position 18 lies in[20, 30), giving 20+(18−12)×10/8=27.5. Grouped percentiles are estimates. Compare medians and IQR, and identify outliers separately.

title: Location, spread and transformations
task: For 2, 4, 4, 5, 20 find mean, median and mode. Predict what adding 3 or multiplying by 2 does to mean, variance and standard deviation.
solution: Mean 7, median 4, mode 4. Adding 3 increases the mean by 3 and leaves variance/SD unchanged. Multiplying by 2 doubles mean/SD and multiplies variance by 4. Grouped mean/SD use class midpoints and are estimates.

title: Pearson correlation and regression
task: Fit the regression explorer's default points. Predict y at x=3 andx=8. Explain the difference in reliability and why correlation is not evidence of causation.
solution: y=2x, r=1; predictions 6 and 16. x=3 is interpolation, 8 is extrapolation beyond observedx=1…5. Confounding variables or coincidence can create associations.

title: Probability and expected frequency
task: List the sample space for two coin tosses. Find the probability of at least one head and its expected frequency in 200 independent trials.
solution: HH, HT, TH, TT. For a fair coin the probability is 3/4=1−P(TT); expected count 150. Actual frequency varies.

title: Combined events and conditional probability
task: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue counters. Draw twice without replacement. Draw a probability tree, calculate P(RR) and P(second red | first blue), and explain dependence.
solution: P(RR)=(3/5)(2/4)=3/10. P(second red | first blue)=3/4, which differs from the original 3/5. Branch probabilities change after removing a counter. Use a Venn diagram or table for unions and intersections.

title: Discrete distributions and expectation
task: Prizes 0, 5, 20 have probabilities 0.6, 0.3, 0.1. Find a fair entry fee and expected net gain if the fee is 4.
solution: Expected prize=3.5, so the fair fee is 3.5. At fee 4 the expected net gain is−0.5. The probabilities must be non-negative and sum to 1.

title: Binomial models
task: For X~B(3, 0.5), find P(X≥2), mean and variance. Explain the four modelling conditions and when repeated draws without replacement violate them.
solution: P(X≥2)=0.5, mean 1.5, variance 0.75. Fixed number of trials, two outcomes, independence and constant success probability are required; removing items generally changes the success probability.

title: Normal models and inverse probabilities
task: For X~N(50, 10²), find P(40≤X≤60) and the 90 th percentile. Explain why a continuous variable has P(X=50)=0.
solution: Probability≈0.682689; 90 th percentile≈62.8155. Probability is area over an interval, and a single point has zero width. About 95% and 99.7% lie within two and three standard deviations.

title: Spearman rank correlation
task: Use the rank explorer to create a large final observation. Explain why Pearson changes while Spearman may stay unchanged, and how ties are ranked.
solution: Pearson uses magnitudes; Spearman uses ordering. If the rank order does not change, the rank correlation stays fixed. Assign ties their average occupied rank and correlate the ranks.

title: Hypothesis tests
task: Compare the hypotheses, assumptions and decisions for a chi-square independence test, a goodness-of-fit test, and a pooled unpaired two-sample t-test. Repeat at 1%, 5%, 10% significance.
solution: Independence tests association; goodness-of-fit tests category proportions; a t-test compares population means. Use expected counts>5 and df>1 for these chi-square activities. The t-test assumes independent samples from normal populations with equal unknown variances. Reject H₀ when p≤α; failing to reject is not proof of equality. Choose one/two tails before seeing results.

title: Derivative as a limiting rate
task: For f(x)=x² at x=2, compare secant slopes forh=1, 0.1, 0.01 and predict the limiting slope.
solution: Slopes 5, 4.1, 4.01 approach 4=f′(2). The derivative describes an instantaneous rate with output-units per input-unit.

title: Increasing and decreasing functions
task: For f=x³−3x, identify the intervals of increase and decrease from the derivative sign.
solution: f′=3x²−3: positive for x<−1 orx>1, negative for−1<x<1. A zero derivative alone does not decide whether a function changes direction.

title: Power-rule differentiation
task: Differentiate 3x⁴−2x⁻²+7 and find the derivative at x=1.
solution: 12x³+4x⁻³; at 1 the derivative is 16. The original function and its derivative exclude x=0.

title: Tangents and normals
task: For y=x² at x=2 find tangent and normal equations. Explain what happens to the normal at x=0.
solution: Tangent y−4=4(x−2); normal y−4=−(x−2)/4. Atx=0 the tangent is horizontal and the normal is the vertical line x=0.

title: Antiderivatives and definite integrals
task: Given f′=3x²+2 and f(0)=5, find f. Evaluate the integral of 3x²+2 from 0 to 2 and interpret its area.
solution: f=x³+2x+5. Integral=[x³+2x]₀²=12. The integrand is positive, so the integral equals the area between the graph and the x-axis.

title: Stationary points and extrema
task: Classify the stationary points of x³−3x and compare with x³ at zero using changes of derivative sign.
solution: At−1, positive to negative gives a local maximum; at 1, negative to positive gives a local minimum. Forx³ the derivative is positive on both sides of 0: a stationary inflection.

title: Optimization in context
task: With 40m of fencing for three sides against a wall, derive the area function, state a physical domain and justify the maximum using derivative signs and endpoints.
solution: A(w)=w(40−2w), 0≤w≤20. A′=40−4w changes positive to negative atw=10; area 200m². Endpoint areas are 0; physical positive-area designs use 0<w<20.

title: Trapezoidal approximation
task: Approximate the integral ofx²+1 from 0 to 4 with one and two strips, compare with the exact value, then explain the direction of the error.
solution: One strip 36; two strips 28; exact 76/3≈25.3333. The chords lie above this convex graph, producing an overestimate; this direction is not universal for other curves.
